source.title: GroupBERT: Enhanced Transformer Architecture with Efficient Grouped Structures
source.authors: Ivan Chelombiev; Daniel Justus; Douglas Orr; A. Dietrich; Frithjof Gressmann; Alexandros Koliousis; C. Luschi

record.file_problem: none; the full paper, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures validation MLM loss across model sizes and SQuAD performance across sizes, but does not fit or evaluate the original scaling-law equations.
record.gate_note: Figure 4 reports validation MLM loss against pre-training FLOPs for multiple model sizes, but the text gives no plotted loss values or power-law fits. Table 4 reports SQuAD scores by model size. Table 1 reports architecture-ablation MLM losses; those results are recorded as findings outside the versions because the architecture variants are not compared at a fixed parameter count. Cited scaling-law results are not recorded as this study's findings.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture-efficiency paper comparing GroupBERT with BERT. It uses size sweeps (29M–516M parameters, about one order of magnitude) and Kaplan-style MLM validation loss to draw Pareto frontiers for its own method. It fits no power law, extrapolates nothing, searches no compute-optimal allocation, and does not relate downstream scores to loss or scale predictively. SQuAD scores rising across four sizes is incidental and not a test of predictability.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude GroupBERT is up to 2.1x more efficient in FLOPs and time-to-train, with better pre-training and SQuAD results across sizes. GroupBERT Base beats BERT Large on MLM loss using 47% of its resources. They also say the advantage grows with model size.
record.recipe_differences: This is an architecture-efficiency study, not a reproduction of the original scaling-law method; it compares GroupBERT and BERT model families and reports loss and downstream scores.
record.method_sensitivity: Model family and size vary; ablation results also vary with architecture changes and learning rate. Fine-tuning scores use selected hyperparameters after sweeps.

fits_no_version.finding: SQuAD v1.1 F1/EM rises monotonically from Small to Large in both BERT (73.2→84.2 F1) and GroupBERT (76.8→85.5 F1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuned SQuAD scores increase monotonically with BERT-family model size over 29M–516M parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: Authors state GroupBERT's advantage over BERT grows with model size; this rests on figure-only results.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture improvements can shift the loss-vs-FLOPs frontier by an amount that grows with scale.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablations of the study's own method: convolution and GFFN modules lower MLM loss while also adding parameters and FLOPs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Not a scaling-law claim; these are the study's own method results.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code will be made publicly available.
record.problems: Figure 4's loss values are not stated numerically in the text, and no power-law fit is reported. Architecture-ablation comparisons are confounded by changes in parameter count, FLOPs, and sometimes learning rate. The paper reports standard deviations for plotted MLM and fine-tuning results but gives no uncertainty values in Table 4.

untested.parts: No power-law fit or exponents. The size range is only about one order of magnitude, with no token or compute scaling isolated.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
Text MLM only; no other modalities or regimes.
No predictive fit of downstream score against scale or loss; only four sizes, each with a best-hyperparameter score.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from the reader's tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. The paper cites Kaplan et al. only to choose MLM validation loss as its metric and to motivate scaling. All size sweeps serve to compare the study's own architecture against BERT.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not fit or report power-law exponents, test token-count scaling independently, establish behavior over several orders of magnitude, or isolate regimes where parameters, tokens, or compute are not bottlenecks.
No predictions from small runs are compared with substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute search over parameter and token allocations is reported.
Architecture ablations are reported, but not at a fixed parameter count across a wide range of depth, width, or other architecture choices.
The study concerns English text pre-training and fine-tuning; it does not test other modalities or the listed alternative training regimes.
The study reports SQuAD scores by model size, but does not fit a predictive relationship between downstream performance and pre-training loss.
The study does not compare scaling-law fitting choices, exponents, or curve bending.
